title: Dangerous, But Not Dangerous Enough to Fix
hook: Omaha yards can hold enough lead to harm a child and still fail to qualify for cleanup — because the rule that decides who gets help was written to a 1994 understanding of the risk.
key_points: A remediation standard is a numeric threshold: cross it and the government acts, fall below it and you are on your own, however real the harm.
The EPA's Omaha cleanup standard — replace soil above 400 parts per million of lead — was set in 2009 using health recommendations from 1994.
An EPA risk model later found soil must be under 100 ppm to protect most children under current health guidance; the CDC has twice lowered what counts as a high blood-lead level.
Flatwater Free Press and ProPublica tested 388 homes inside the Omaha Superfund site and found 208 above 100 ppm — dangerous by today's science, ineligible under the 400 ppm rule.
Cost is the core objection: a 2024 study estimated cleaning every US home above 100 ppm would run $500 billion to $1.4 trillion, and proposed capping soil instead of digging it out.
Thresholds move with politics — Biden's EPA lowered the national screening level to 100 ppm in 2024; the Trump administration raised it to 200 ppm the following year.
content_html: Regulation usually comes down to a number. Somewhere in a rule is a threshold — parts per million, decibels, micrograms — and that number quietly decides who gets helped and who is told their problem does not count. Omaha shows what happens when the number stops matching what scientists know.
extra_html:
The federal government has been pulling lead out of Omaha's yards since the late 1990s, after elevated blood-lead levels in children were traced to a smelter and downtown factories that had spread lead dust for over a century. The rule governing that work says contractors dig up and replace a yard if it tests above 400 parts per million of lead. It was set in 2009 — on health recommendations from 1994. Since then the evidence on low-dose exposure has hardened, the CDC has twice lowered what it treats as a high blood-lead level, and an EPA risk model concluded that protecting most children under current guidance means getting soil below 100 ppm. When the Flatwater Free Press and ProPublica, reporting with Chris Bowling, tested 388 homes inside the Superfund site, 208 came back over 100 ppm. They are hazardous by today's science and invisible to the rule.

Why the rule has not moved is the instructive part, and it is not simply neglect. Roughly 40% of US homes exceed 100 ppm; a 2024 study by leading soil-lead researchers estimated $500 billion to $1.4 trillion to remediate them all, and argued for capping contaminated soil with clean soil or mulch as a cheaper path. Thresholds also swing with each administration: Biden's EPA lowered the recommended national screening level to as little as 100 ppm in 2024, and the Trump administration raised the lowest screening level to 200 ppm the next year, saying it wanted to speed cleanups of the highest-risk areas. Meanwhile other governments picked stricter numbers — Norway and Minnesota act at 100 ppm, California screens at 80. The EPA notes that soil removal is only one tool, pointing to the Omaha Lead Registry and a county lead-prevention program, and is retesting the area with findings expected by October 2027. The general lesson travels well beyond lead: a standard is a frozen judgment about acceptable risk and affordable cost, and keeping it current is a political act, not an automatic one.

related.title: Who Checks Whether a Cleanup Held?
related.hook: The EPA remediated 13,000 Omaha yards and moved on. Reporters retested 620 of them for $10 a sample — and found lead above the agency's own trigger in four of every ten.

related.title: Environmental Governance
related.hook: How do you regulate something that ignores borders and belongs to no one? Environmental governance is the toolkit societies use to manage nature collectively.

related.title: What Public Policy Is
related.hook: Passing a law is just the start. Public policy is the whole arc — from defining a problem to actually delivering a solution and seeing whether it worked.

related.title: Markets, Regulation & the Mixed Economy
related.hook: Pure free market or full state control? Almost every country picks neither — they run a mixed economy, and where they draw the line is one of politics' great arguments.

flashcards.prompt: Why can a hazard be well documented and still not qualify for government cleanup?
flashcards.back_html: Because eligibility is set by a numeric threshold written at some past moment. If the science moves and the number does not, real harm can sit legally below the line that triggers action.

flashcards.prompt: What creates the Omaha "gap" the reporting describes?

choices.text: Cleanup is triggered at 400 ppm of lead, but an EPA model says protecting most children requires soil under 100 ppm
The EPA has no lead standard for the site at all
Residents are barred from testing their own soil

flashcards.explanation_html: Yards between 100 and 400 ppm are risky under current health guidance yet fall below the threshold that obliges the agency to replace the soil.

flashcards.prompt: What is the main argument the reporting gives against cleaning all US soil to 100 ppm?

choices.text: Cost — a 2024 study put it at $500 billion to $1.4 trillion, and suggested covering soil rather than removing it
Evidence that lead below 400 ppm is harmless
A lack of laboratories able to measure lead that precisely

flashcards.explanation_html: About 40% of US homes exceed 100 ppm, so the researchers argued for the cheaper option of capping contaminated soil with clean soil or mulch.
